title: Emrys and the Cellar
premise: Beatrix Yarrow's late-night radio show, 'The Hollow Signal,' has always been a refuge for the strange—until callers begin phoning in who died the week before, each one asking her to remember them. When an excavation crew beneath her studio unearths a cellar door sealed from the inside, Beatrix discovers her predecessor, a 1974 host named Emrys Vane, made a bargain with something below: he fed it names to keep his own, and Beatrix's voice is the inheritance she never wanted. To break the cycle she must return what was taken—the recorded voices of the dead, including Emrys himself—and open the door from the outside. In the end, Beatrix survives by giving up the show, the archive, and her anonymity, broadcasting the truth once before walking away as the cellar finally goes quiet.
about_author: Juniper Nystrom is a former community radio volunteer from coastal Maine who spent three years archiving dead-air recordings before turning to fiction. 'Emrys and the Cellar' is her second novel, written mostly between midnight and four in the morning.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Beatrix hosts another uneventful night of 'The Hollow Signal,' taking calls from insomniacs and cranks. Her last caller, a woman named Dolores, mentions details of Beatrix's childhood no stranger could know. Beatrix archives the call out of habit. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: uneasy normalcy, the first hairline crack.

chapters.title: The Obituary Page
chapters.summary: Beatrix cross-references last week's obituaries and finds Dolores among the dead. Two more callers match. She plays the tapes back and hears a faint third voice underneath hers on every recording. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into obsession; documentation becomes compulsion.

chapters.title: Excavation
chapters.summary: The construction crew renovating the station's foundation hits something: a door of blackened oak, sealed shut from the inside, set into raw earth where no cellar should be. The foreman wants it bricked over. Beatrix feels the building hum through her shoes. POV: Beatrix with a brief crew-foreman interlude. Emotional beat: the past physically surfacing.

chapters.title: Emrys Vane, 1974
chapters.summary: In the station's flooded basement archive, Beatrix finds reels labeled in a dead man's hand: E. VANE, FINAL BROADCAST. She learns Emrys hosted her exact time slot fifty years ago and vanished mid-show, leaving eleven minutes of tape that are just breathing. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: kinship with a ghost; she is not the first.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: The dead callers multiply. A drowned boy asks Beatrix to tell his mother he wasn't scared. She does, and the mother hangs up on her. Beatrix realizes the calls only come when she's on air—her voice is the door now. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: compassion weaponized against her; guilt begins its work.

chapters.title: The Station Manager
chapters.summary: Manager Ruth Okonkwo confronts Beatrix about ratings anomalies—listenership spiking at 3 a.m., then flatlining. Ruth reveals the station has quietly changed owners five times since 1974, each sale dated days after a host quit or disappeared. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: institutional rot; power has been managing this thing for decades.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Beatrix deciphers Emrys's logs hidden inside reel cases: in 1974 he bargained with the thing below, feeding it recorded voices of the recently dead in exchange for his career, then his life. The voices were never returned. The debt compounds. POV: Beatrix reading Emrys's words. Emotional beat: horror reframed as theft; someone must give it back.

chapters.title: Dolores
chapters.summary: Dolores calls again, lucid for the first time, and explains the rules: the thing below eats memory, not flesh. The dead forget themselves down there unless someone above remembers them aloud. Beatrix is the remembering. That's why she was chosen. POV: Dolores. Emotional beat: tenderness inside terror; found family among the dead.

chapters.title: Ruth's Bargain
chapters.summary: Beatrix finds Ruth's name in Emrys's ledger—not as victim but as signatory. Ruth renewed the arrangement years ago to save the station from bankruptcy, feeding it a single name: her brother's. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: corruption revealed in someone Beatrix trusted; survival has a price everyone pays differently.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Beatrix descends to the door alone with a recorder. Through the oak she hears hundreds of voices reciting their own names like prayers, thinning as they forget. One voice says hers. It knows her. It has been waiting for her specifically. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the trap closes; invisibility was never possible.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Wasn't Scared
chapters.summary: Beatrix tracks down the drowned boy's mother and tells the truth off-air. The mother, shattered, gives Beatrix a box of his belongings—including a cassette he mailed the day he died, addressed to 'the radio lady.' POV: alternating Beatrix and the mother. Emotional beat: grief shared is grief halved; the living can be family too.

chapters.title: Interference
chapters.summary: The thing below escalates: every radio within a mile plays Beatrix's old shows back at her, edited so she confesses things she never said. Neighbors begin looking at her strangely. Her anonymity—the armor she built her life around—dissolves. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: exposure as violation; power corrupting her public voice.

chapters.title: Emrys Speaks
chapters.summary: During broadcast, the third voice under her tapes resolves into Emrys Vane, alive in some diminished way, apologizing. He explains how to return the voices: play every stolen recording back into the earth, all at once, at the door. But the door opens both ways. POV: Emrys via tape. Emotional beat: the predecessor's guilt passed like an inheritance.

chapters.title: Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: Beatrix compiles the full list—two hundred and six names across five decades—and realizes returning the voices will free the dead but end the show, the station, and possibly her. Ruth refuses to help; her brother's voice is down there, and she'd rather he be kept than lost. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the cost itemized; resolve hardening.

chapters.title: What Ruth Kept
chapters.summary: Beatrix broadcasts Ruth's confession without permission, forcing the truth into daylight. Ruth, ruined and furious, finally grieves her brother instead of hoarding him—and hands Beatrix the master key to the transmitter room. POV: Ruth. Emotional beat: betrayal as mercy; corruption broken by shame and love.

chapters.title: The Last Request Line
chapters.summary: Beatrix opens the phones and tells her listeners everything. Most hang up. But dozens stay, strangers volunteering to read names on air all night—a chorus of the living holding up the dead. POV: Beatrix and multiple callers. Emotional beat: found family realized; she is no longer invisible and no longer alone.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: At 3 a.m., Beatrix carries the archive reels to the door while the volunteers read names on air, keeping the dead anchored. The door, sealed from the inside for fifty years, unlocks at the sound of its own history being spoken. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into ceremony.

chapters.title: Return
chapters.summary: Beatrix plays the voices back into the dark, one by one, two hundred and six times. Each returned voice takes a piece of her memory as toll—her mother's face, her first winter, her own middle name. She keeps going. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the price of survival paid in selfhood.

chapters.title: Emrys
chapters.summary: Last of all comes Emrys, who begs her to stop—to let him stay, because what remains of him is only the show, and ending means erasure. Beatrix tells him he was more than his broadcast, and sends him home. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: the climax's moral heart; refusing the corruption that took him.

chapters.title: Eleven Minutes
chapters.summary: The door slams. The building exhales. Beatrix climbs out missing pieces of herself, guided up by the volunteers' voices still reading names overhead. On air, she plays Emrys's final eleven minutes of breathing, then lets the silence run. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: exhaustion, hollowed-out peace.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Beatrix broadcasts one final show: the whole story, names included, her confession and the town's. Then she signs off forever, surrendering the frequency, the archive, and the voice that made her a vessel. The dead do not call again. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: release; documentation completed, prayer answered.

chapters.title: The Quiet Frequency
chapters.summary: Months later, Beatrix lives unnamed in a coastal town, working a day job, missing memories she'll never recover but sleeping soundly. Late one night, a stranger's radio crackles with a woman's voice thanking listeners for remembering. Beatrix smiles, doesn't pick up the phone, and turns it off. POV: Beatrix. Emotional beat: bittersweet coda; some doors stay closed because we choose to close them.
